clue.text: Were gardener and park one and the same?

definitions.note: the answer names a single person with two natures, the phrase describes that pairing

blocks.note: Gertrude Jekyll was a famous English garden designer
taken as written
Hyde Park is the large royal park in central London

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a famous gardener and a London park could secretly be the same thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude Jekyll and Hyde Park are unrelated, but Stevenson's Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde really were one man.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's novella the respectable doctor and the brutal Hyde turn out to be a single person with a split personality.

clue.text: Can you recall how Morse was christened? Try!

blocks.note: first meaning: the detective's long-hidden first name
second meaning: to make an effort, attempt

explanation.surface: A quiz question about the first name of Inspector Morse, urging the contestant to have a go.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter's Inspector Morse kept his first name secret for years; it was finally revealed as Endeavour.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to attempt or strive, so it can stand for an exhortation to try.

clue.text: Long greatly to make brass at start of Yule

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
brass is British slang for money, so making brass is earning

explanation.surface: Someone longs to make plenty of money in time for Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brass' is northern British slang for money. 'at' places the earning after the first letter of Yule.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to feel an intense longing or desire for something.

clue.text: Heather came first: I'm not sure who is next

indicators.note: what comes next follows on behind, so one piece is placed after the other

blocks.note: to come first is to lead, past tense led
um is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: A girl called Heather was first in line, and the speaker cannot say who follows her.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather looks like a girl's name in a queue, but it is the plant. Ledum is a genus of shrubs in the heather family, including Labrador tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Ledum is a genus of evergreen ericaceous shrubs, botanical relatives of heath plants.

clue.text: Pests enter Kelly, but let's not be vexed

indicators.note: whatever enters something ends up inside it

blocks.note: vermin are pests such as rats
Ned Kelly was the famous Australian bushranger

explanation.surface: Pests have got into someone called Kelly's place, but they say not to worry.
explanation.walkthrough: Ned Kelly, the armoured nineteenth-century Australian outlaw, supplies the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dismissive 'don't worry about it', urging someone not to be bothered.

clue.text: Catch that jarred Number Ten, to pay for fire?

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase describing what the noun was for

indicators.note: something jarred is jolted and shaken out of its order

blocks.note: to catch what is said is to hear it
taken as written
X is the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: A political question about Downing Street raising money to heat the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number Ten' suggests Downing Street, but it is only the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: The hearth tax was a seventeenth-century English levy charged on each fireplace in a household.

clue.text: Meet most of cost, what food is governed by?

definitions.note: a description of the government department rather than a synonym

indicators.note: most of something is all but a small part, so its final letter goes

blocks.note: to defray costs is to meet or pay them; the following 'cost' completes the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone asks who should pay most of the bill for regulating our food.
explanation.walkthrough: DEFRA is the UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which oversees food policy.
explanation.definitionFit: The British ministry responsible for agriculture and food standards regulates the national supply of things we eat.

clue.text: From four fawns' game it's not a hundred yet

definitions.note: a cryptic description of the answer, not a synonym

indicators.note: something made from materials is reworked out of them into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Four young deer playing a game, of a sort that has not yet lasted a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like the definition or the indicator but is part of the letters. When this appeared in 2005, British women's first parliamentary vote, in 1918, was not yet a century old.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes for women came to Britain in 1918, so at the time of publication the right had not reached its centenary.

clue.text: Void at the outset, asks "they leave nought dry?"

indicators.note: something put out of place is disordered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a void is a blank, an empty space
read as 'out' plus 'set': the second half supplies these letters
to pray is to ask earnestly, as in 'pray tell'

explanation.surface: Someone at the start of a blank page wonders aloud about whatever soaks everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Araucaria splits 'outset' into 'out' and 'set': the second half is rearranged by the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A blanket spray covers an entire area, so nothing in its path escapes being wetted.

clue.text: A game of cards men may have left in lurch

definitions.text: men may have left in lurch

blocks.note: first meaning: a children's card game in which you try not to be left holding the odd queen

blocks.clueFragment: men may have left in lurch
blocks.note: second meaning: an unmarried woman passed over by suitors

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a dated description: a woman whom men left unmarried, in the lurch.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a card game where one player ends with the unmatched card and an old term for a spinster.

clue.text: Amount of drug that makes sixth boy turn left

blocks.note: VI is the Roman numeral six
Alf is a boy's name
a U-turn, so U stands for turn
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A dose of medication that makes a sixth-former suddenly veer off to the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sixth boy' reads as a sixth son, but sixth gives only the numeral and the boy is a separate name. U for turn comes from U-turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A vialful is the quantity that a small medicine bottle holds, a measure of a dose.

clue.text: A profit that I mean to multiply?

definitions.note: the definition is a cryptic hint; 'as much again' means doubled

blocks.note: taken as written
profit is money made, what you come out ahead by

explanation.surface: An investor talks about a profit they hope to grow many times over.
explanation.walkthrough: Saying a sum is 'as much again' means doubling it, so the word itself carries a sense of multiplying.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb signals repetition: doing something once more or adding as much again, which is a form of multiplying.

clue.text: Old second version's many a humorous text

blocks.note: first meaning: a second version is a Mark Two, and twain is the old word for two
second meaning: the American author of numerous comic books

explanation.surface: An old revised edition contains plenty of funny writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Two labels a second model or version; 'Old' asks for the archaic form of two. The 's then reads as 'is', and the author is the books he wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Samuel Clemens, whose comic novels and sketches make him stand for a body of humorous writing.

clue.text: South German wine from contact with the live?

definitions.note: a cryptic description of what touching a live wire gives you

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
hock is the British name for German white Rhine wine

explanation.surface: A wine from southern Germany produced by close contact with something lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the live' sounds like living vines, but it is the live wire carrying electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Touching a live electrical conductor sends current through the body, which is an electric jolt.

clue.text: Cook that won martial - also poster - fame

definitions.text: that won martial - also poster - fame

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for someone who works in a kitchen

blocks.clueFragment: that won martial - also poster - fame
blocks.note: second meaning: the British field marshal famous for victories and a recruiting poster

explanation.surface: A cook who became famous both as a soldier and as the face on a poster.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Kitchener won battles in Sudan and South Africa, and his pointing face headed the 1914 'Your Country Needs You' recruiting poster.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun once meant a kitchen worker, and it is also the surname of the celebrated British field marshal.

clue.text: See 16 down
Twice quit a crude plan forged of four or five

definitions.note: the two answers are matched loosely in turn to the numbers, quadr- and quint-

indicators.note: something forged is hammered into a new shape

blocks.note: the word written out two times
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a rough scheme two times over, a plan put together by four or five people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' doubles the word that follows it before everything is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin roots point to square (four sides) and five: quadratic relates to squaring, quintuple means fivefold.

clue.text: China makes obvious cover for gold church

indicators.note: a cover goes around whatever it protects, so one piece wraps the rest

blocks.note: plain means obvious, clear to see
or is the heraldic term for gold
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: China openly provides protection for a church's golden treasures.
explanation.walkthrough: China looks like the country, but it is the crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine ceramic tableware is called china after the country where the material was first made.

clue.text: Scots head in mouth, plus it's from mouth of horse

indicators.note: the head of anything is its top, so only its opening letter is used
one thing is put inside another

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
a firth is a Scottish river estuary, a river's mouth
plus means and

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's head ends up in a mouth, and someone heard it straight from the horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots' primes the solver for the Scottish word: firths such as the Firth of Forth are estuaries. 'From the horse's mouth' is an idiom for direct, reliable information.
explanation.definitionFit: Information received directly from the original source, without intermediaries, is said to come straight from the horse's mouth.

clue.text: Unknown leaves king supply of wine to get

definitions.note: the town that supplies sherry, standing for the wine itself

indicators.note: whoever leaves goes away, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: x is the algebraic unknown
Xerxes was a king of ancient Persia

explanation.surface: A mysterious stranger abandons the king, taking the royal wine cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: The Persian king loses one of his two Xs, the middle one, to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Xeres is the old name of Jerez in Andalusia, home of sherry, and the old word for that fortified wine.

clue.text: It's Archer faked old German legislature

indicators.note: something faked is concocted, made up into a false form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An accusation that Archer forged documents, in a nod to the novelist-politician's perjury.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, the British novelist and Conservative peer, was jailed in 2001 for perjury, which gives 'faked' its sting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reichsrat was an imperial council: the parliament of Austria and a federal chamber in Weimar Germany.

clue.text: No longer suspect, making Chanel tire

indicators.note: making something is creating it out of raw material, so these letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashion detective drops a suspect, leaving the Chanel house exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tire' reads as weary, but it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been exonerated is free of suspicion, no longer under investigation or in danger.

clue.text: The river tour may be a Cornish feature

indicators.note: what may be something is a possible version of it, so these letters can be rearranged

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat trip up the river might be one of Cornwall's attractions.
explanation.walkthrough: Truro is the cathedral city and county town of Cornwall, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornwall's only city is a landmark of the county, so calling it a Cornish feature is fair.

clue.text: See 21
Goddess, see (say) the rest from X

indicators.note: to say a word is to speak it, so what is wanted is its sound
the rest is what remains once the named letter has been taken off

blocks.note: the letter C is pronounced like 'see'
the answer at 19 across, which begins with that letter

explanation.surface: A goddess is told to look at what remains after something marked with a cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X' looks like a cross or a ten, but it points at 19 across; dropping that letter leaves the rest of the Spanish wine town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceres was the Roman deity of agriculture and grain, a goddess in the classical pantheon.

clue.text: Georgian belief that catches prey, of course

definitions.note: a description of the noun: a net used in hare coursing

blocks.note: GA is the abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
a tenet is a principle or belief

explanation.surface: An eighteenth-century conviction that naturally ensnares its victims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Georgian' suggests the period of the four Georges, but it is the US state. 'of course' is a pun on coursing, the hunting of hares with dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: A gate net was stretched across a gateway in hare coursing or poaching so that fleeing game would run into it.

clue.text: No Scout, old king of learning was bereft

blocks.note: first meaning: the Scout motto is 'Be Prepared', so a non-Scout is unprepared
second meaning: the nickname of the Anglo-Saxon king Ethelred

explanation.surface: A boy who was never a Scout, like an ancient monarch, lacked an education.
explanation.walkthrough: Ethelred the Unready ruled England around 1000; his epithet originally meant 'ill-advised'. The tail adds that being unread means lacking learning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means unprepared, failing the Scout motto, and is the traditional epithet of King Ethelred II.

clue.text: Such marks on road result in -brass or -brule

definitions.note: a description of hybrid animals, not a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: black and white stripes painted where pedestrians cross
second meaning: breeding the striped animal with an ass gives a zebrass, with a mule a zebrule

explanation.walkthrough: The dangling endings are completed by the first part of the answer: interbreeding the striped animal with an ass or a mule produces the hybrids zebrass and zebrule.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the striped British pedestrian crosswalk and, literally, the cross-breeding of the African animal.
